title: Function Flow Canvas
user: Engineers onboarding to an unfamiliar service who need to follow one request path across functions, files, and types without opening an unbounded set of editor tabs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In an Ask HN thread about wished-for developer tools, a commenter asks for a function call graph where clicking a call opens its callee with relevant calls and structs highlighted.
The 35-reaction CodeGraph roadmap consolidates ongoing requests for source-code graph support across many languages, underscoring the cross-language nature of code navigation demand.

recurrence: A direct 2025 request plus a 2026, 35-reaction language-support tracker; the pain recurs whenever a developer must form a local mental model of a large code path.
current_workaround: Use editor go-to-definition/back stacks, manually split tabs, draw temporary diagrams, or ask a teammate for a tour.
incumbents_and_gap: VS Code and JetBrains expose call hierarchies, while CodeGraph provides broad indexing. None makes a deliberately small, task-scoped, shareable path canvas from one chosen function the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI using an installed language server to emit one self-contained HTML canvas for a selected symbol: inbound/outbound calls, type hops, source snippets, and collapsible depth. Non-goals: repository-wide AI search, code editing, or hosted code indexing.
success_measure: In a pilot, 70% of users can answer a five-step request-path question in under ten minutes after generating a canvas, versus their documented baseline.
monetization: one-time — a local analysis utility has episodic, high-value use and should not require source upload or a recurring seat fee.
constraints: Parse locally; support only language servers that are already installed; exclude generated/vendor paths by default; never send source code to a service.
why_distinct: It is a constrained code-reading artifact, not another IDE, code graph database, or LLM codebase chat.

title: API Scenario Patch
user: Small API teams that need to review a realistic, multi-step request scenario in Git without sharing a hosted API-client workspace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster reports Postman capping free team collaboration at one user; replies recommend plaintext, Git-tracked request collections as an alternative.
A Bruno user requests saving multiple payload/parameter sets for one API call so tests can be switched without rewriting or losing prior data.

recurrence: Two independent API-client communities in late 2025 and 2026 describe lost scenario context and the cost of hosted collaboration limits.
current_workaround: Duplicate requests in Postman/Bruno, paste curl commands into pull requests, or maintain loosely related JSON files and README notes.
incumbents_and_gap: Postman and Insomnia optimize interactive clients; Bruno stores collections locally. The gap is a reviewable patch containing an ordered scenario, extracted variables, redacted observed responses, and reviewer notes — not a whole client workspace.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI/proxy that records an opted-in sequence of HTTP exchanges, replaces configured secrets with placeholders, extracts selected response values into named variables, and writes a deterministic Markdown plus YAML scenario patch. Non-goals: being a REST client, cloud collaboration suite, or API test framework.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilot scenario patches are reviewed in a normal pull request without a reviewer asking for an external workspace or copied credentials.
monetization: free — Git-native interoperability and trustworthy local redaction are stronger adoption levers than a paid collaboration gate.
constraints: Default-deny recording of authorization headers, cookies, and bodies; redact JSON paths before writing; make replay explicit and disabled by default.
why_distinct: The product captures a reviewable change narrative for an API flow; it does not compete to replace the user's everyday HTTP client or duplicate a fixture matrix runner.

title: Agent Secret Capsule
user: Developers allowing a coding or browser agent to use a narrowly scoped credential who need the command to succeed without exposing the raw credential in prompts, terminal output, or tool traces.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly asks how to secure local secrets when agents need broad local access and prompt injection or tool misuse makes the machine no longer feel trusted.
An Infisical user reports a Mac agent repeatedly printing Cloudflare keys while performing a task, even after being told to stop revealing secrets.

recurrence: A direct security-practice request and a concrete 2026 secret-disclosure incident show both anticipated and observed severity.
current_workaround: Put secrets in environment variables, give an agent broad shell access, manually redact output, use a separate sandbox, or prohibit the action altogether.
incumbents_and_gap: 1Password, Doppler, Infisical, and OS keychains store secrets; agent sandboxes isolate environments. The missing small layer is a per-command secret lease with output scrubbing and an auditable expiry receipt.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that injects a selected secret only into a named subprocess or localhost credential broker, strips exact and encoded values from captured stdout/stderr, expires the lease, and writes a no-value receipt. Non-goals: secret-manager replacement, browser automation, or autonomous approval of new scopes.
success_measure: Across 100 controlled agent-tool invocations, no configured secret appears in captured terminal output while 95%+ of authorized calls complete successfully.
monetization: one-time — security-sensitive local tooling benefits from an inspectable binary and no recurring access tax.
constraints: Use the OS keychain where available; warn that redaction cannot prevent exfiltration through an authorized network call; protect against shell history and child-process inheritance; no telemetry by default.
why_distinct: It governs one agent action and its observable output, rather than storing another copy of the team's secrets.

title: Release Env Fingerprint
user: Engineers shipping the same service through local, CI, staging, and production environments who need to find missing, extra, or differently resolved configuration without revealing values.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A local-first secret-manager builder cites .env values being shared in Slack, committed to Git, drifting across machines, and breaking deployments without a clear audit trail or rollback.
A GitHub Docs issue describes a self-hosted versus hosted runner environment-variable context difference that can cause workflow failures.

recurrence: Both a 2025 CI context failure and a 2026 developer report identify configuration drift as a release problem, not merely a secret-storage preference.
current_workaround: Compare .env files by hand, print variable names in logs, maintain spreadsheets, or discover the mismatch only after a failed deploy.
incumbents_and_gap: Doppler, Infisical, 1Password, and dotenvx distribute secrets. They do not provide a portable release-time fingerprint that proves configuration shape and selected safe invariants match across execution contexts.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that captures a name/type/presence fingerprint from an approved command, compares signed fingerprints by environment, and enforces rules such as required prefixes, endpoint host allowlists, and value hashes for explicitly non-secret values. Non-goals: secret storage, deployment, or reading values back from cloud secret managers.
success_measure: A pilot catches 90% of seeded missing/renamed/context-only variables before deployment while recording no secret value in its report.
monetization: free — broad shell and CI compatibility matters more than centralizing sensitive deployment configuration.
constraints: Never persist raw environment values; salt hashes per project; explicitly classify allowlisted non-secrets; support POSIX shell and GitHub Actions first.
why_distinct: It verifies the shape and safe properties of a release environment instead of becoming another vault or dotenv file manager.

title: Migration Commit Witness
user: Backend teams reviewing SQL migrations who need a concrete record of what committed, what rolled back, and which rollback claim was actually exercised before production.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a 23-comment Ask HN thread on reviewing and deploying SQL, users describe Git/Liquibase workflows but note that teams are often poor at ensuring changelogs have a usable revert capability.
A Flyway issue reports a deferred constraint violation at commit that leaves DDL created while the migration is incorrectly marked successful.

recurrence: The review thread and a current migration-engine failure expose the same high-severity boundary: a green migration tool result is not necessarily a safe, reversible database state.
current_workaround: Rely on migration framework status, review raw SQL in a pull request, keep manually written rollback notes, and inspect a disposable database after the fact.
incumbents_and_gap: Flyway, Liquibase, Atlas, and ORM migrations apply and track changes. They do not center a portable before/after commit witness that checks transaction boundaries, schema/data assertions, and an optional exercised rollback.
smallest_useful_product: A CI CLI that runs an existing migration command against a disposable database, snapshots selected schema/data invariants before and after commit, optionally runs a supplied rollback, and emits a signed Markdown/JSON witness. Non-goals: generating migrations, replacing a migration engine, or touching production databases.
success_measure: In seeded CI cases involving deferred constraints and non-transactional DDL, the witness flags every partial-commit outcome that the underlying migration command reports as successful.
monetization: one-time — teams can adopt it per repository and retain the evidence artifact without subscribing to a database intermediary.
constraints: Only use ephemeral/test credentials; require explicit rollback scripts; database dialect behavior must be labeled rather than generalized; never auto-run rollback in production.
why_distinct: It independently proves migration outcomes and rollback claims; it is not a competing migration DSL or schema-diff product.

title: CI Outage Witness
user: Maintainers of critical GitHub Actions pipelines who need an evidence bundle that distinguishes a repository failure, runner failure, and platform degradation when logs are delayed or absent.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN report says GitHub Actions runs stretched from 5–10 to 20–30 minutes and sometimes failed with no logs while the public status page showed no issue.
A 116-reaction runner issue reports vague 'Runner not found' failures across several self-hosted architectures, restarts, and token exhaustion without a clear cause.

recurrence: Independent hosted and self-hosted reports in 2025 show that opaque CI failures can consume maintainer time and trigger misleading retries.
current_workaround: Refresh GitHub status, rerun jobs, inspect scattered runner journals, paste screenshots into incidents, or wait for a provider acknowledgement.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub Actions provides run pages and status history; Datadog and Better Stack monitor external services. Neither creates a compact, repository-owned witness that correlates queue, runner, API, log-availability, and retry evidence for one failed run.
smallest_useful_product: A GitHub CLI extension that snapshots run metadata, job transitions, available logs, runner diagnostics, GitHub status components, and retry lineage into one redacted incident bundle. Non-goals: replacing CI, auto-retrying jobs, or claiming root cause from insufficient evidence.
success_measure: For 20 pilot incidents, maintainers classify the failure as code, runner, or probable platform degradation within 15 minutes in at least 80% of cases.
monetization: free — incident bundles are most useful when every open-source and small-team maintainer can attach them without a monitoring subscription.
constraints: Use read-only GitHub scopes; strip tokens, repository secrets, and log lines matching configured patterns; label status observations with their timestamp and uncertainty.
why_distinct: It is an after-the-fact diagnostic receipt for a single CI incident, not an uptime monitor or CI dashboard.

title: WebMCP Safety Check
user: Web teams exposing WebMCP/browser automation tools who need to inspect which operations can mutate state, use a real profile, or access an origin before an agent is allowed to call them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN discussion shows developer confusion about how WebMCP is reachable and what browser-resident tool calls mean in practical deployments.
The MCP proposal says browser-automation servers vary on fresh versus real browsers, origin-scoped credentials, human approval, and before/after evidence, with no standard discovery mechanism.

recurrence: WebMCP adoption questions and a protocol-level safety-contract proposal in 2026 point to a new, concrete inspection need before browser agent exposure broadens.
current_workaround: Read prose tool descriptions, trust server defaults, manually inspect scripts, or disable browser automation entirely.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser DevTools inspect network activity and MCP Inspector exercises protocol traffic. Neither gives a product owner a policy-oriented inventory of declared browser-agent safety properties and missing claims.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension plus CLI that reads a WebMCP/MCP manifest or session transcript, classifies tools by read/mutate/external-navigation/credential scope, and fails CI on missing approval or evidence declarations. Non-goals: executing agent tasks, scraping pages, or deciding whether a vendor is trustworthy.
success_measure: In a test corpus of tool manifests, the checker identifies every intentionally omitted mutation/approval declaration and generates a review card in under one minute.
monetization: free — an open policy format needs ecosystem adoption; paid compliance packs could be considered only after a standard settles.
constraints: Treat server declarations as claims, not proof; avoid collecting browser content; track the evolving WebMCP/MCP specifications without inventing compatibility guarantees.
why_distinct: It is a static/sessional safety inspector for browser-agent surfaces, not an MCP server, agent, or generic browser automation product.

title: Journey Failure Receipts
user: Teams using Playwright for critical user journeys who need the exact visual and DOM state at each failed soft assertion, not only the page state after the test finishes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer built synthetic monitoring after a client's site returned 200 while its Add to Cart flow was broken for six hours because of a silent JavaScript error.
A Playwright feature request asks for screenshots at each expect.soft() failure because the HTML report currently shows only the final page state.

recurrence: A production false-green incident and a current Playwright request identify the same loss of diagnostic evidence in browser-flow testing.
current_workaround: Capture a final trace/video, add ad-hoc screenshots around assertions, rerun a flaky flow interactively, or inspect a page that has already moved past the failure.
incumbents_and_gap: Playwright offers traces, videos, and HTML reports; Checkly and Datadog run synthetic checks. The gap is a tiny reporter that emits an assertion-level, scrubbed evidence receipt for the test suite teams already run.
smallest_useful_product: An npm Playwright reporter/helper that captures screenshot, selected DOM/accessibility snapshot, console errors, network summary, and masked form state at each configured soft assertion, then emits one static receipt per failure. Non-goals: hosted monitoring, test orchestration, or visual-regression replacement.
success_measure: In a pilot set of failed journey tests, engineers identify the failing UI state without rerunning the test in at least 75% of cases.
monetization: free — an open test reporter should be easy to install in CI; paid retention would be a separate future service.
constraints: Mask selectors and fields before capture; cap artifacts; make network bodies opt-in; ensure receipts do not expose credentials or customer data in CI artifacts.
why_distinct: It improves the evidence granularity of existing browser tests instead of offering another synthetic-monitoring dashboard.

title: Restore Drill Attestor
user: Indie SaaS operators and small platform teams who need repeatable proof that a database backup can restore into an isolated target and pass application-specific sanity checks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A backup-service validation thread notes that backup urgency often appears only after a major outage, while small teams lack resources to manage backup tooling.
A 22-reaction Restic issue details the operational complexity of append-only backup protection and the need for a separate trusted management host in compromise scenarios.

recurrence: The 2025 small-team concern and the high-interest backup-security discussion both show that retained backups do not equal an operationally trustworthy recovery path.
current_workaround: Trust a cloud snapshot badge, run a manual restore during an incident, or maintain a fragile shell script with no durable evidence.
incumbents_and_gap: RDS snapshots, pgBackRest, WAL-G, Restic, and managed backup services create backups. They do not provide a vendor-neutral drill runner that records an isolated restore, user-defined health checks, cleanup, and a compact attestation.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that invokes an existing restore command into a disposable container/database, runs declarative row-count/schema/application checks, destroys the target, and writes a timestamped attestation with durations and no data values. Non-goals: storing backups, replacing backup engines, or promising ransomware protection.
success_measure: A pilot team completes a scheduled restore drill in under 20 minutes and can show an attestation no older than 30 days for each protected database.
monetization: one-time — recovery verification should remain portable even if the team's backup provider changes.
constraints: Require isolated non-production targets and explicit destructive-target confirmation; never copy production data to a shared service; use encrypted local temporary storage only when unavoidable.
why_distinct: It validates recovery and produces evidence; it neither stores data nor tries to become a backup vendor.

title: SQLite Workload Lab
user: Developers shipping SQLite, FTS5, or SQLite extensions who need reproducible performance and CPU-compatibility evidence before publishing an optimization claim or binary release.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer benchmarking SQLite FTS5 PRAGMAs says repeated tests made them less certain of the results and how to describe them.
A sqlite-vec issue reproduces a release wheel crashing with SIGILL on older x86_64 CPUs because build-machine AVX/AVX2 flags leaked into published artifacts.

recurrence: The 2025 FTS measurement uncertainty and a 2026 binary-compatibility regression show that a SQLite workload result needs reproducible workload, build, and hardware context.
current_workaround: Write one-off benchmark scripts, paste timings into a README, test on the developer's own CPU, or find compatibility failures after release.
incumbents_and_gap: sqlite3's shell, hyperfine, Criterion, and benchmark frameworks time commands; package CI builds artifacts. The gap is a SQLite-aware lab record combining PRAGMAs/schema/workload, explain plans, CPU feature matrix, and portable result comparison.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that executes declarative SQLite workloads in containers or QEMU profiles, captures SQLite version/compile options/PRAGMAs/query plans/CPU flags, and generates a diffable Markdown/JSON report. Non-goals: a database ORM, hosted benchmark farm, or automatic query tuning.
success_measure: A release candidate is tested against at least three declared CPU profiles and a regression greater than 15% is detected from a committed baseline in CI.
monetization: free — transparent, reproducible benchmark records are valuable precisely when they can be checked by open-source maintainers.
constraints: Clearly separate emulator from hardware results; pin SQLite builds and fixture data; do not claim statistically significant improvements without repeated-run methodology.
why_distinct: It is a reproducibility and portability harness for SQLite workloads, not another SQLite GUI or vector database.

title: Log Duplicate Lens
user: Operators of Loki or JSON log pipelines who need to quantify accidental duplicate ingestion across streams before it distorts search results, alert counts, and storage cost.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team asks for a logging SaaS that can ingest and query logs quickly, while replies describe expensive/overcomplicated alternatives and difficult configuration tradeoffs.
A 13-reaction Loki issue explains that automatic stream sharding can put resent identical log lines in different streams, defeating normal de-duplication.

recurrence: The general 2025 difficulty of choosing usable logging and a concrete 2025 Loki duplicate-ingestion mechanism make log amplification a costly, easily missed operational problem.
current_workaround: Manually search log windows, infer duplicates from message text, adjust labels/retries, or accept inflated volume and noisy alerts.
incumbents_and_gap: Loki, Elasticsearch, Datadog, and OpenObserve search and retain logs; they do not make a bounded duplicate-amplification investigation and remediation hint a small local diagnostic workflow.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that samples Loki JSON exports or newline-delimited logs, fingerprints messages with configurable timestamp tolerance, groups cross-stream near-duplicates, estimates volume/alert inflation, and emits label/retry evidence. Non-goals: log ingestion, hosted retention, or deleting records from a provider.
success_measure: On labeled sample data, the tool finds at least 90% of intentionally duplicated events and keeps false-positive groups below 5% after configured normalization.
monetization: one-time — an offline investigation tool should operate on an export without retaining a customer's logs.
constraints: Sample and process locally; support redaction before reports; do not infer that identical messages are erroneous without presenting the stream/retry evidence; handle high-cardinality inputs with bounded memory.
why_distinct: It diagnoses a specific amplification failure mode in an existing log stack, rather than becoming another log platform or dashboard.

title: API Profile Guard
user: Developers switching API requests among development, staging, and production who need an unmistakable, policy-checked preflight before a request uses the wrong base URL, environment file, or credential class.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster says default API tooling is cloud based, offline alternatives are moving toward subscriptions, and asks whether the fallback is curl.
A 12-reaction Bruno request asks for seamless .env.dev/.env.staging/.env.prod switching rather than the current single workspace .env file.

recurrence: 2026 API-tool pricing/control frustration and a separate multi-environment workflow request point to a persistent unsafe context-switching gap.
current_workaround: Rename .env files, use separate collections, edit base URLs by hand, rely on color conventions, or fall back to curl with copied variables.
incumbents_and_gap: Postman, Bruno, Insomnia, and dotenv tools store or select environments. They do not provide a standalone, client-agnostic preflight policy that can block a destructive request based on the resolved profile while keeping secret values local.
smallest_useful_product: A local proxy/CLI wrapper that resolves named env files, displays a non-secret profile fingerprint, validates host/method/path/body policies, requires an explicit production acknowledgement, and logs a no-value receipt. Non-goals: an HTTP client GUI, secret vault, API gateway, or request history cloud.
success_measure: In a seeded test set, the guard blocks 100% of requests aimed at a forbidden production host or missing required profile variable before any network connection is opened.
monetization: free — a cross-client safety convention needs low-friction adoption and must not force users into another API platform.
constraints: Never log headers or bodies by default; profile parsing must not execute shell expressions; provide explicit allowlists for production operations; work without a network connection except for the guarded request.
why_distinct: It adds a portable safety checkpoint around existing clients and curl, not a new REST client or another API test suite.
